title: Shape the data once: tables
summary: Searching a file again on every line is slow work. Read it once into a table, declare -A or awk, and each line becomes one lookup.

scheme: while read -r customer item qty; do
on every line:  $( ) starts a process
text: bill.sh is only one loop: n orders, n turns. Still, 1 000 orders take 1.4 seconds, because each turn is expensive.
- Each line starts three programs: about a millisecond together, far more than looking a price up.
- grep reads prices.txt from the top every time: the same file parsed again and again.
- 20 000 orders: about 30 seconds, for a few hundred kilobytes.
Read the file once, and keep it in the shape your question needs: a table from item to price.
- declare -A makes an associative array: each key (a name) leads to its value.
- ${price[$item]} finds the value by its key: no file to read, as fast with 10 items as with 100 000.
- Needs bash 4 or newer: macOS's /bin/bash 3.2 has no -A.

scheme: while read -r item cents; do        ← once
while read -r customer item qty; do ← n turns
script: while read -r customer item qty; do
text: Two loops, one after the other, not one inside the other.
- 20 000 orders: 0.2 s instead of about 30, each file read once.
- Inside $(( )), price[$item] reads the table: no $ needed in front.

- An item missing from the table gives 0 there, and $(( )) reads the value as arithmetic: 0250 is octal, text can run commands. When the file comes from outside, check first: [[ -v price[$item] && ${price[$item]} =~ ^(0|[1-9][0-9]*)$ ]].

scheme: NR    line number, all files together
FNR   line number in this file
NR == FNR:  first file only → fill
then each order:  look up, multiply
text: awk has tables built in, and reads both files in one program.
- NR == FNR is true only during the first file: awk fills the table there, and next skips to the next line.
- On orders.txt, price[$2] is a lookup, then a multiplication.
- Careful: if prices.txt is empty, NR == FNR stays true on orders.txt.

scheme: is x in the list?   list          read it all
what's x's price?   table (key)   one step
in both lists?      sorted lists  one walk
Python: dict        SQL: index, a few steps
text: The data is the same; the shape you give it decides the work.
- A list answers by reading it: n steps for each question.
- A table answers by key: one step, whatever its size.
- Two sorted lists answer “in both?” in one walk, side by side: that is what comm and join do.
- Shape the data once, before the loop. Then ask as many questions as you like.
A table is only as good as its key: one key for each thing you look up.
- Cut the key short and two items share it: the last one read wins, without a word.
- Same with a key taken from a column that repeats, like a first name.
- Before you trust a table, ask: can two lines give the same key?
